sections.title: Key topic 1: The development of the civil rights movement, 1954–60

topics.title: 1 The position of Black Americans in the early 1950s

points.point_text: **Racial segregation, social discrimination & voting rights in Southern states.**: Jim Crow Laws: Southern states legally enforced racial segregation in schools, transit & public accommodations; Voter Disenfranchisement: Authorities used arbitrary literacy tests, poll taxes & violent intimidation to prevent Black citizens from registering to vote; Separate but Equal: The 1896 Plessy v. Ferguson Supreme Court ruling established this legal doctrine, though Black facilities were consistently inferior

topics.title: 2 Progress in education and legal challenges

points.point_text: **The causes, core features & historical impact of the Brown v. Topeka ruling (1954).**: Supreme Court Ruling: Chief Justice Earl Warren led a unanimous (9-0) decision declaring that segregated public schools violated the 14th Amendment's Equal Protection Clause; Doctrine Overturned: The court declared that separate educational facilities are 'inherently unequal,' dismantling the constitutional basis for Jim Crow; Southern Resistance: Southern politicians signed the 'Southern Manifesto' & formed White Citizens' Councils to delay & block school integration

points.point_text: **The causes, key developments & importance of the desegregation crisis at Little Rock Central High School (1957).**: Faubus' Defiance: Arkansas Governor Orval Faubus deployed the state's National Guard to block nine Black students from enrolling at Central High School in Little Rock; Federal Intervention: President Eisenhower federalized the Arkansas National Guard & sent the 101st Airborne Division to escort the students to classes; Cold War Context: Eisenhower intervened partly to defend the nation's international reputation, as Soviet propaganda weaponized images of racial violence

points.point_text: **Resistance to desegregation in the South, focusing on the Dixiecrats & the formation of White Citizens' Councils.**: Dixiecrats: Southern conservative Democrats who strongly defended segregation & opposed federal intervention under the banner of 'states' rights.'; White Citizens' Councils: Middle-class segregationist groups that used economic intimidation, job firings & boycotts to suppress civil rights activists

sections.title: Key topic 2: Protest, progress and radicalism, 1960–75

points.point_text: **The impact of the Greensboro sit-ins & the growth of the student movement.**: Greensboro Sit-in (1960): Four Black college students sat at a segregated Woolworth's lunch counter, refusing to leave after being denied service; Rapid Spread: This action sparked a wave of sit-ins across the South, involving over 70,000 students & desegregating hundreds of public counters; SNCC Founded: The movement led directly to the creation of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) to coordinate student protests
points.teacher_note: ⚠️ UNEXAMINED TOPIC: Not assessed in the 2018–2025 public exam series. Prime territory for upcoming classroom mocks and revision.

points.point_text: **The causes, key events & impact of the Freedom Rides (incl. white supremacist violence & the Anniston bus bombing (1961).**: CORE Campaign: Activists rode interstate buses into the deep South to test federal rulings outlawing transit segregation); Anniston Bombing: An angry white mob firebombed a Freedom Riders' bus in Anniston, Alabama & beat the escaping passengers; Federal Action: The extreme violence forced Attorney General Robert Kennedy to issue a strict ban on transit segregation
points.teacher_note: ⚠️ UNEXAMINED TOPIC: Not assessed in the 2018–2025 public exam series. Prime territory for upcoming classroom mocks and revision.

points.point_text: **The desegregation of the University of Mississippi & the James Meredith case (1962).**: Ole Miss Desegregation: James Meredith won a federal court order to enroll at the all-white University of Mississippi; Federal Force: Governor Ross Barnett physically blocked him, sparking riots that forced President Kennedy to send 30,000 federal troops to secure Meredith's safety
